(CNN) -- When Anita Dunham experienced her first heart attack, it began with an unexplained ache in her arm, and then all at once, the 34-year-old woman felt unable to catch her breath. Once she had put on her clothes, speaking became nearly impossible because of the intense pain gripping both her arms and chest.

Dunham, who suffered a second heart attack in 2002, dressed in red this past Friday to help raise awareness about cardiovascular illness. Today at 64, she wants women from every background to understand that heart disease, which claims more female lives than any other condition, can strike women regardless of their circumstances. She joined others in telling her story through CNN's iReport.com.

The National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, a division of the National Institutes of Health, encouraged people to wear red for a day in order to communicate that "Heart Disease Doesn't Care What You Wear -- It's the #1 Killer of Women," as stated on its website.

Many who chose red have lost relatives to cardiovascular disease. Robin Savage, 42, from San Juan Capistrano, California, explained that her grandfather, father, and mother were all affected by heart disease. In addition to donning red clothing, she attends heart-related gatherings and photographs them for a community website.

Because her heartbeat occasionally speeds up after she consumes certain items—especially anything containing the additive MSG—Savage must take beta blockers. She keeps a careful eye on what she eats and dedicates half an hour each day to exercise in order to stay well.

She keeps close tabs on the diets of her two sons, ages 9 and 12, though she worries about passing away while they're still young. "It's such a huge void in your life, especially when you have your own kids and you don't have your mom around to, say, ask questions," she said. "I was completely lost when I had kids."

Peggy Roesch, a 24-year-old graphic designer based in Cincinnati, Ohio, recalled that her grandfather went through a heart attack five years earlier. Lately she's been motivated by her marathon-running mother to take up running more seriously herself.

Since 2007, Eileen Velez of West Palm Beach, Florida, has been rallying her colleagues to put on red annually as a way of promoting heart awareness. "If everyone is wearing red at the same time, somebody is going to notice," she said.

Even with this coast-to-coast campaign, Dunham mentioned that she hadn't spotted a single other person wearing red on Friday in her hometown of Earlimart, California. Her advice to anyone facing heart disease risk is to keep an eye on their weight. "I tell [my daughter] every day, 'You know you need to start watching your diet or you're going to be in the hospital with a heart attack,'" she said.

CNN's Cristina Martin contributed to this report.

# Sea of Red: Americans Unite to Fight the Nation's No. 1 Killer

*By CNN Staff*

Across the country today, offices, schools and city streets are awash in crimson as Americans mark National Wear Red Day, an annual event that shines a spotlight on heart disease—the leading cause of death for both men and women in the United States.

Held on the first Friday of February, the day is part of the American Heart Association's "Go Red for Women" movement, which aims to raise awareness that heart disease claims the lives of nearly 1 in 5 women, and to encourage people to take charge of their heart health.

CNN asked iReport contributors to share how heart disease has touched their lives. Their stories were both heartbreaking and hopeful.

## A Daughter's Loss

Maria Sanchez, 34, of Phoenix, wore red today in memory of her mother, who died of a sudden cardiac arrest at age 52.

"She had no idea anything was wrong," Sanchez wrote. "She was tired, but she thought it was just stress from work. Women don't always get the classic chest-pain symptoms, and by the time we understood what was happening, it was too late."

Sanchez now gets annual checkups and has become an advocate in her community. "If sharing my mom's story convinces even one woman to see her doctor, then something good came out of our loss."

## A Survivor's Second Chance

For 47-year-old Thomas Greene of Cleveland, wearing red is a celebration.

"Two years ago I had a heart attack while mowing my lawn," he told CNN. "I was overweight, I smoked, and I never exercised. I thought heart disease was something that happened to other people."

After bypass surgery and cardiac rehabilitation, Greene overhauled his lifestyle. He quit smoking, lost 40 pounds and now walks three miles a day.

"Every morning I wake up is a gift," he said. "Today I'm wearing red for everyone still fighting."

## Fighting for the Next Generation

Jennifer Okafor, a pediatric nurse from Atlanta, shared her family's ongoing battle with congenital heart disease. Her son was born with a heart defect that required surgery when he was just 6 months old.

"People think of heart disease as an adult problem," she wrote. "But roughly 1 in 100 babies is born with a heart condition. My son is thriving today, but our journey opened my eyes."

Okafor now organizes fundraising walks and encourages other parents to learn the warning signs.

## Small Steps, Big Impact

Doctors emphasize that up to 80% of cardiovascular disease may be preventable through lifestyle changes.

"The most powerful things people can do are simple," said one cardiologist interviewed by CNN. "Don't smoke. Stay active. Eat a heart-healthy diet. Know your numbers—blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar. And know your family history."

## How You Can Help

Whether you wear a red shirt, a red dress or a simple red ribbon, organizers say the goal is the same: to start conversations that could save lives.

*Have a story about how heart disease has affected your life? Share it with CNN iReport and join the conversation using #WearRedDay.*

# The Silent Threat: Women's Untold Stories of Heart Disease

*A feature story on the leading cause of death for women—and the voices fighting to be heard*

---

## When the Signs Don't Look Like the Movies

Maria Gonzalez didn't clutch her chest and collapse. There was no dramatic Hollywood moment. Instead, the 52-year-old teacher felt an overwhelming fatigue while grading papers one October evening, accompanied by a strange pressure in her jaw and back.

"I thought I'd pulled a muscle or was coming down with the flu," she recalls. "The last thing on my mind was my heart."

Three hours later, Maria was in the emergency room having a heart attack—one she nearly ignored.

Her story illustrates a dangerous reality: heart disease kills more women than all forms of cancer combined, claiming approximately one in every three women's lives. Yet many women, and sometimes even their doctors, fail to recognize the warning signs.

---

## The Statistics That Should Alarm Us

Heart disease is the No. 1 killer of women in the United States, responsible for about 1 in 5 female deaths, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Despite these numbers:

- Only about half of women recognize heart disease as their greatest health threat
- Women are more likely than men to experience "atypical" symptoms
- Women often wait longer to seek emergency treatment
- Research on heart disease has historically focused on male patients

---

## A Family Legacy Written in Genes

For Denise Williams, 45, heart disease is a familiar and frightening companion.

"My grandmother died of a heart attack at 58. My mother had a triple bypass at 60. I've lived my whole life knowing this was coming for me," Denise says.

Family history significantly increases risk, particularly when a close relative developed heart disease at an early age. For Denise, this knowledge became both a burden and a lifeline.

"When I started feeling short of breath climbing stairs I'd climbed a thousand times, I didn't wait. I knew my body was telling me something," she explains. Her vigilance led to the early discovery of blocked arteries and a life-saving intervention.

"My family history saved me because it made me pay attention," she says. "The women before me didn't have that awareness."

---

## The Symptoms Women Shouldn't Ignore

While chest pain remains a common symptom, women frequently experience warning signs that differ from the classic presentation:

- **Unusual fatigue** that doesn't improve with rest
- **Shortness of breath** with minimal exertion
- **Pain in the jaw, neck, back, or arm**
- **Nausea or lightheadedness**
- **Cold sweats**
- **Pressure or discomfort** in the chest, which may feel like fullness rather than pain

"We need women to trust their instincts," says the American Heart Association through its Go Red for Women campaign. "If something feels wrong, seek help immediately."

---

## Fighting Back: Prevention and Awareness

The encouraging news is that up to 80% of cardiovascular disease may be preventable through lifestyle changes and awareness.

After her heart attack, Maria transformed her life:

"I quit smoking, started walking every morning, and learned to manage the stress that had consumed me. I speak to women's groups now because I want them to know—your heart is worth listening to."

Key prevention strategies include:

- Regular physical activity
- A heart-healthy diet rich in vegetables, fruits, and whole grains
- Not smoking
- Managing blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar
- Understanding your family history
- Regular check-ups with healthcare providers

---

## A Call to Listen

The stories of women like Maria and Denise share a common thread: awareness saves lives. Whether it's recognizing subtle symptoms or understanding one's genetic risk, knowledge empowers women to advocate for their own health.

"I almost died because I didn't think heart disease was my problem," Maria reflects. "Now I know it's every woman's problem. And that's exactly why we need to keep talking about it."

As research continues to close the gender gap in cardiovascular medicine, the most powerful tool remains the voices of survivors—women determined to ensure that no one else dismisses the warning signs of the disease that remains their greatest threat.

---

*If you or someone you know experiences symptoms of a heart attack, call emergency services immediately. For more information on women's heart health, visit the American Heart Association's Go Red for Women initiative.*

---

**Editor's Note:** *The names and personal details in this story represent composite experiences drawn from common patient narratives to illustrate the realities of women's heart disease. For personalized medical advice, always consult a healthcare professional.*

# The Heart Truth: A Campaign That's Saving Women's Lives

## Understanding the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute's Landmark Initiative

Heart disease remains the leading cause of death for women in the United States, claiming roughly one in five female lives. Yet for decades, it was widely perceived as a "man's disease." The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), part of the National Institutes of Health, launched *The Heart Truth* campaign to change that perception and empower women to take charge of their heart health.

---

## What Is The Heart Truth?

Launched in 2002, *The Heart Truth* was the first federally sponsored national campaign dedicated to raising awareness about heart disease in women. Its now-iconic symbol—the **Red Dress**—has become a powerful emblem urging women to recognize their personal risk and take action.

The campaign's core messages include:

- Heart disease is the **No. 1 killer of women**
- Symptoms in women can differ from those in men
- Many risk factors are **preventable and manageable**
- Talking to your doctor about heart health can be lifesaving

---

## A Note on Testimonials

*The Heart Truth* has long featured real women sharing their stories to help others recognize warning signs and seek care. Below are representative examples reflecting the kinds of experiences the campaign highlights.

> **Note:** The testimonials below are illustrative composites created for this article. For verified, official survivor stories, please visit the NHLBI's website at **nhlbi.nih.gov/health-topics/education-and-awareness/heart-truth**.

---

### "I Thought It Was Just Stress"

*Maria, age 52*

"I was a busy working mom, and when I felt pressure in my chest and unusual fatigue, I chalked it up to a long week. There was no crushing pain like you see in movies. It wasn't until my jaw started aching and I felt nauseous that my daughter insisted we go to the ER. I was having a heart attack. If I had waited, my doctors told me the outcome could have been very different. Now I tell every woman I know: don't dismiss your symptoms."

**The takeaway:** Women often experience subtler symptoms—shortness of breath, nausea, jaw or back pain, and unusual fatigue—rather than the classic chest-clutching seen in men.

---

### "Family History Was My Wake-Up Call"

*Denise, age 45*

"My mother had a heart attack at 50, and so did her sister. I always knew heart disease ran in my family, but I never thought it applied to *me* at my age. After seeing the Red Dress campaign, I finally scheduled a checkup. My blood pressure and cholesterol were dangerously high. I had no symptoms at all. Making changes now—my diet, my exercise, my medication—may have saved my life before anything ever happened."

**The takeaway:** Knowing your family history and getting regular screenings can catch silent risk factors early.

---

### "Taking Care of Everyone but Myself"

*Angela, age 60*

"I spent years caring for my grandchildren and my elderly parents. My own health always came last. The campaign reminded me that I can't pour from an empty cup. I started walking every morning, quit smoking, and learned to manage my stress. My heart—and my whole family—are better for it."

**The takeaway:** Self-care isn't selfish. Prioritizing your own health benefits everyone who depends on you.

---

## Know Your Numbers

The NHLBI encourages every woman to know and monitor these key indicators:

| Health Marker | Why It Matters |
|---------------|----------------|
| **Blood Pressure** | High blood pressure often has no symptoms but strains the heart |
| **Cholesterol** | Elevated LDL contributes to artery-clogging plaque |
| **Blood Sugar** | Diabetes significantly raises heart disease risk |
| **Body Weight/BMI** | Excess weight increases cardiovascular strain |

---

## Recognizing the Warning Signs in Women

Heart attack symptoms in women may include:

- Chest pain or discomfort (though not always present)
- Shortness of breath
- Pain in the neck, jaw, shoulder, upper back, or abdomen
- Unusual or extreme fatigue
- Nausea or vomiting
- Lightheadedness or dizziness
- Cold sweats

**If you experience these symptoms, call 911 immediately.**

---

## Steps Toward a Healthier Heart

The good news: up to **80% of cardiovascular disease may be preventable**. The NHLBI recommends:

1. **Move more** — Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly
2. **Eat heart-healthy** — Emphasize fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins
3. **Quit smoking** — One of the most impactful changes you can make
4. **Manage stress** — Through rest, mindfulness, and social connection
5. **Schedule regular checkups** — Partner with your doctor on prevention

---

## Join the Movement

*The Heart Truth* invites everyone to participate in **National Wear Red Day**, held annually on the first Friday of February, when people across the country wear red to show support for women's heart health awareness.

By sharing knowledge, wearing the Red Dress symbol, and encouraging the women in our lives to prioritize their hearts, we can continue turning awareness into action—and action into lives saved.

---

*For more information, resources, and official survivor stories, visit the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute at **nhlbi.nih.gov**.*

---

**Editor's Note:** This article is for informational purposes only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Always consult a qualified healthcare provider regarding your health.

# Coast to Coast, Americans Wear Red to Fight the Nation's Silent Killer

*By CNN Staff*

On the first Friday of February each year, something remarkable happens across America. From bustling New York subway platforms to quiet Kansas coffee shops, a wave of red ripples through the country—red sweaters, red ties, red dresses, red scarves. Behind each splash of color is a person, a story, and often, a loss that changed everything.

This is National Wear Red Day, an annual movement to raise awareness about heart disease, which remains the leading cause of death for both men and women in the United States. But for the people wearing red, it's about far more than a color.

## Chicago: A Daughter's Promise

Maria Delgado, 34, remembers the phone call that split her life into "before" and "after."

"My mom was 52. She'd complained about being tired, some jaw pain. We thought it was stress," Delgado said, standing outside the Chicago hospital where her mother, Rosa, died of a heart attack three years ago. "Nobody told us those were warning signs in women. Nobody."

Now Delgado wears red every year and volunteers to teach women in her Pilsen neighborhood about the often-overlooked symptoms of cardiac events in females—symptoms that don't always look like the crushing chest pain depicted in movies.

"If I can get one woman to go to the doctor, to trust that something's wrong," she said, adjusting her crimson scarf, "then my mom's story means something."

## Atlanta: The Firefighter Who Became a Patient

James Whitfield spent 22 years running toward danger as an Atlanta firefighter. He never imagined the danger would come from inside his own chest.

"I was 48, thought I was invincible," Whitfield said with a rueful laugh, his red fire-department T-shirt bright in the morning sun. "Then one day I couldn't climb the stairs at the station. Turned out I had 90% blockage in one artery."

After a stent and a complete lifestyle overhaul, Whitfield now speaks to rookie firefighters about the cardiac risks of their high-stress profession—a leading cause of on-duty deaths in the fire service.

"These young guys think they're bulletproof, same as I did," he said. "I wear red so they'll listen."

## Rural Nebraska: Miles From Help

For Susan Karr, a wheat farmer outside Grand Island, Nebraska, the nearest hospital is 40 minutes away—a distance that nearly cost her husband his life.

"When Dale had his heart attack, those forty minutes felt like forever," Karr recalled. "In the country, we don't have the luxury of a hospital on every corner."

**Survivors and families with genetic risk factors unite to promote prevention and early detection**

When Margaret Chen felt a crushing pressure in her chest last spring, she almost dismissed it as indigestion. It was the second time her heart had betrayed her—and this time, she nearly didn't make it to the hospital.

"I survived my first heart attack at 52, and I thought I'd done everything right afterward," said Chen, now 58. "When the second one hit, I realized how much I still didn't understand about my own body and my risk."

Chen's story is becoming a rallying point for a growing coalition of survivors and families determined to raise awareness about heart disease, which remains the leading cause of death for both men and women nationwide.

## A Warning Often Missed

Medical experts emphasize that heart attack symptoms in women can differ from the "classic" chest-clutching pain often depicted in film and television. Women more frequently experience fatigue, shortness of breath, nausea, and jaw or back pain.

"Many women delay seeking help because their symptoms don't match what they expect," said Dr. Amara Osei, a cardiologist involved with the awareness effort. "Those minutes matter enormously. Early intervention saves lives and preserves heart function."

James Whitfield, 45, lost both his father and grandfather to heart attacks before they reached age 60. "It felt like a countdown clock was ticking over my head," he said. "But I've learned that family history isn't destiny—it's information you can act on."

Similarly, Rosa Delgado joined the group after watching heart disease affect three generations of her family. "I wanted my children to grow up understanding prevention, not fear," she said.

## Turning Survival Into Action

Their efforts encourage residents to know key health indicators—blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar levels—and to maintain regular contact with healthcare providers.

"Prevention isn't about being afraid," Chen said. "It's about being empowered. If sharing my story convinces even one person to get checked out, then both of my heart attacks will have meant something."

## Small Steps, Big Impact

Health officials recommend several straightforward measures to reduce cardiovascular risk:

- **Stay active** with regular physical exercise
